title: The Beggar
text:
In one of his short prose poems, Turgenev describes walking along a street when an old beggar stopped him. The man was frail and pitiful: red, tearful eyes, blue lips, rough rags, filthy sores. Poverty had eaten him away. He held out his swollen, red, unwashed hand and moaned, asking for help.

The narrator began searching through his pockets. He found no purse, no watch, not even a handkerchief. He had taken nothing with him. And the beggar went on waiting, his outstretched hand trembling slightly.

Confused and ashamed, the narrator took the dirty, trembling hand in his own and pressed it warmly. "Do not be angry with me, brother," he said. "I have nothing with me, brother."

The beggar raised his inflamed eyes to him. His blue lips smiled, and he in turn squeezed the narrator's cold fingers. "Never mind, brother," he said. "Thank you for this as well. This too was a gift, brother."

And the narrator understood that he, too, had received a gift from his brother.
lesson: When you cannot give anything material, you can still give respect, warmth and your full attention. People feel that as a gift.
source: Ivan Turgenev, Poems in Prose (Senilia), The Beggar (1878)
